title: Sociology 101, taught by Jalen Brunson, Lionel Messi and the Tartan Army
content:
PHILADELPHIA — As soon as the Ivory Coast’s Amad scored against Ecuador in the 90th minute of Sunday’s World Cup match, a tiny spot of orange jerseys in a sea of yellow that dominated that night’s crowd at Lincoln Financial Field erupted in joy.

And when the final whistle sounded in the Elephants’ 1-0 win, that small but passionate fan section was a scene of ecstasy. Fans whipped out their phones to video-call friends watching at 1 a.m. abroad. Someone put their arm around my shoulder and put me on the phone with their family in the Ivory Coast. Exiting the stands, fans began an impromptu dance party, which continued all the way back to the nearest train station.

It brought to mind a term more familiar in college classrooms than sports stadiums: collective effervescence. That is, the otherworldly feeling you get in a crowd of strangers operating as one.

“It’s not enough to just be in the same space,” said Christina Simko, an associate professor of sociology at Williams College, where she taught me the term. “They (members of a crowd) have to have a common focus and a common mood, and through that physical interaction, they generate something … greater than the sum of its parts. That’s this feeling of collective effervescence, this emotional electricity or excitement that lifts people outside of themselves and makes them feel like they’re connecting to something transcendent.”

And right now, it’s everywhere.

It’s Knicks fans flooding the streets of New York to celebrate the team’s first NBA title in 53 years. It’s the Tartan Army singing “500 Miles” at a Boston Red Sox game long after the song ended. It’s Ecuador’s fans chanting “Sí se puede” in perfect unison in a packed subway car on their way to the game. It’s street watch parties and packed sports bars and joyous Carolina Hurricanes fans and the Tarps Off shirtless section at St. Louis Cardinals games.

As my colleague Steve Buckley wrote earlier this week: “Something special is happening across North America. More than ever before, we’re stepping outside to join up with other fans to partly root, root, root for the home team, but also to achieve something that’s as miraculous as what Jesus pulled off with the fishes and the loaves.”

That Buckley reached for a religious metaphor is no surprise. Sociology’s founding father, Émile Durkheim, originally coined the term in 1912 — 18 years before the first World Cup and 35 years before the first Basketball Association of America Finals — in an effort to explain the sacred feeling brought forth by religion.

“He proposed that the sacred was formed in those moments when people rose above themselves and became more than individuals, became a collective, and rose above their individual state to become a society as a whole,” said Megan Robb, an associate professor of religious studies at the University of Pennsylvania who teaches a course on sports and religion.

Robb explained that groups require four elements to reach collective effervescence, religious or otherwise. First, there needs to be a collective; individuals cannot achieve effervescence. Second, the group must have extremely strong emotions. Third, there must be “emotional contagion,” as Robb put it — those strong emotions must “seemingly pass from individual to individual in the group instantaneously, almost as if it’s passing by electricity.” And fourth, outlandish or bizarre behavior.

Sound familiar?

The Knicks didn’t need flyers or Instagram graphics telling fans to congregate outside Madison Square Garden. World Cup tourists don’t plan to coordinate outfits. It just happens.

Collective effervescence can explain negative fan behavior, too.

“People will do things in a crowd that they would never do on their own as individuals,” Simko said.

That might explain the dozens of arrests as fans flooded the streets with each Knicks win. It could explain the school buses lit on fire, or the eggs seemingly thrown at Victor Wembanyama or all the fans standing atop light poles (though these days, Robb thinks that particular form of crowd behavior may have moved beyond spontaneous effervescence into ritual).

But it can also explain the joy.

“In the weakening of other types of institutions, fragmentation that characterizes engagement with all other sorts of topics, there is something about sports,” Robb said. “It gives us the power to transcend a lot of those petty differences and feel part of a single community.”

The 1 a.m. wake-ups to make Thursday’s Knicks parade? The Democratic Republic of Congo fans jumping for joy at their World Cup debut (a 1-1 draw against Portugal)? The handmade outfits and face paint and tears shed at the buzzer?

They’re moments that can “allow you to become more than just an individual,” Robb said, “and join into what you would call the soul of society.”
